Monumental ‘90s Megayacht Emerges After a Decade, Asking for a Whopping $86M
23 photos
Photo: IYC
It irrupted in the early 1990s, breaking all rules and proving the impossible, it stayed hidden for almost a decade, and now it’s back, looking just as dazzling as it did the first day. Forever an icon and one of the boldest superyachts ever built (both in terms of design and propulsion), Zeus is true to its name: a deity of superyachts, looking for a new owner.
Few superyachts deserve the iconic status of Zeus – one of the most incredible luxury yachts of all time on all levels. Right now, this masterpiece is back in the spotlight after almost a full decade of mystery. It has never been chartered in its 35 years of existence, and its most recent (and current) owner chose to keep it away from the spotlight since 2017, when it purchased it. Properly maintained and refitted during all these years, Zeus has re-emerged in full glory.
It was one of the superstars of this year’s Monaco Yacht Show in September, joining the lineup for the first time in almost ten years. It was also one of the most expensive superyachts on display, asking for a whopping Є77 million ($86 million) – an enormous price for a yacht from the ‘90s, but fully justifiable, given its unrivaled iconic status.
Zeus was originally named Eco, a wordplay that hinted at the metaphorical meaning of the Spanish word “echo”, and also stood for “Empresa de Comunicaciones Orbitales”, a news channel founded in 1988. The man behind this news channel was the same behind the futuristic yacht, namely Emilio Azcárraga, the Mexican media mogul dubbed “El Tigre” (The Tiger).
Photo: IYC Azcárraga was compared to Rupert Murdoch, but many believe that what he did for the Mexican media (television in particular) is far greater and pioneering. His life and his personality were just as grandiose as his media empire, so they naturally fitted a collection of radically different, bold luxury yachts unlike anything else on the market at that time. The media mogul started small, with a basic 36-meter CRN motor yacht (named Caribe III) in the ‘70s.
From there, he moved to owning twin superyachts built at the same time according to his specifications. Azteca and Paraiso were the first manifestations of Azcarraga’s futuristic vision and opulent taste – built by Feadship, they were dubbed “the greenhouse yachts” because locals actually believed they were giant greenhouses, not yachts . That was mainly because of the unusual glazing on the top decks, which was unprecedented at the time.
A striking glass design would also later become one of the most revolutionary features of the futuristic Eco. As revolutionary as they were, Azteca and Paraiso only paved the way for what would become Azcarraga’s masterpiece: the 74.5-meter (244 feet) superyacht that took years and considerable effort to build because it was such an unusual project, and one that literally developed organically, taking a life of its own.
Azcárraga's original brief changed tremendously and eventually became what was known as Eco – the 1991 megayacht that revolutionized everything that existed in that size category at the time. El Tigre only got to enjoy this masterpiece for a few years, and even spent the final moments of his life onboard Eco. After he passed away in 1997, Eco was purchased by another famous, ultra-rich owner: Larry Ellison.
Photo: IYC Ellison renamed it Katana and made important tweaks to the megayacht, completed by the same original designer. Ellison would go on to own a series of custom-built superyachts based on his own vision, leaving the ’91 Eco behind. In 2004, it was sold to British entrepreneur Aidan Barclay and renamed Enigma. The current owner (reportedly the Monaco-based real estate mogul John Christodoulou) purchased it in 2017, renaming it Zeus.
Azcárraga brought the vision and the money for this masterpiece, but the real genius behind it is Martin Francis, the multi-talented designer that led the entire project (exterior and interior), which is a monumental task in its own. It wasn’t a smooth process, like today’s superyachts that follow a precise brief and are completed in two years, but things worked out in the end, resulting in something bigger (literally and figuratively) than the owner himself first planned.
Zeus became a milestone for almost everyone involved in the process of bringing it to life, from Martin Francis (this was his first motor yacht) and François Zuretti (who had never worked on a yacht interior until then), to the entire team of young designers and architects, some of whom would eventually become iconic names in the industry (most notably, Espen Oeino).
Azcarraga’s first two custom superyachts were built by the Dutch giant Feadship, but for Eco, he tapped Blohm+Voss, a German shipyard, specifically for its experience with gas turbine-powered high-speed vessels. The Blohm+Voss shipyard was later acquired by the Lurssen Group, the biggest German builder of superyachts, where it remains active as a distinctive brand.
The yacht was monumental in size and groundbreaking in design – the unique superstructure with curved panoramic windows became the most recognizable feature of Zeus, one that was never replicated on another yacht and that is just as iconic to this day. The convex-built windows that make Zeus look so striking both inside and out were apparently inspired by French buses.
Photo: IYC For the interior, Azcarraga wanted an Art Deco aesthetic, and the famous François Zuretti worked with Francis to create something that remains iconic to this day. Even 35 years later, Zeus sports the same original interior design, only with careful upgrades such as stone restoration, leatherwork, and new carpets in the guest area (added in 2025).
The massive 1,150 GT volume allowed for a six-stateroom configuration that can accommodate up to 15 guests, attended by an equally massive crew of 21. The elevated Panoramic Salon is one of the most impressive living spaces onboard.
The giant aft deck (later transformed into a basketball court for Ellison) was originally meant to house an impressive selection of toys, including a Maule turbo-prop float plane, a luxurious Riva Aquarama, and even a Harley Davidson.
From the start, Zeus didn’t boast just a radically innovative design, but also one of the boldest technical approaches to propulsion, at a time when that was rare. The high-speed gas turbine option was chosen in order to allow greater speeds of up to 30 knots.
Photo: IYC The complete propulsion system would combine a central GE LM1600 gas turbine (Zeus became the launch customer for this turbine) driving a booster jet (the KaMeWa waterjet was the largest-ever built at that time) with classic twin diesel engines driving wing jets.
In addition to this, the use of underwater foil was also revolutionary at the time, allowing for smooth cruising even at the exceptional speed of 35 knots. Imagine a behemoth megayacht of over 200 feet speeding at 35 knots and still maintaining a vibration-free experience for the onboard guests.
This unique, high-performance propulsion system combined with hydrofoil technology provides up to 28,5000 combined horsepower, resulting in a maximum speed of 35 knots. At an economical speed of just 12 knots, Zeus turns into a long-range beast capable of covering up to 4,000 nautical miles.
To these outstanding capabilities of the original design, subsequent refits added premium zero-speed stabilizers, major work completed on the machinery, waterjet, and navigation, plus communications refit work leading to a fully upgraded bridge.
Photo: IYC When he was still alive and well, Azcárraga tested the yacht’s long-range capabilities by cruising extensively on both sides of the Atlantic. He even traveled with a small tanker named Eco Supporter (similar to today’s shadow yachts built for massive megayachts) that enabled the refueling of the gas turbine during extended cruises.
Back in 1991, Eco was a total disruptor and a pioneer. Today, it remains a huge part of modern yacht design, and ultimately a collector’s item – one that is fully operable and worth more than some of the best brand-new superyacht on the market.
